title: Under the Desert Sky, Counting What I Cannot Count
script: Narrator: [reflective] We'd driven three hours out of the city specifically to escape its glow, and even so, I hadn't quite prepared myself for what greeted us once we stopped.
Narrator: [amazed] The moment I stepped out of the car, the sky simply overwhelmed me, thick with stars in a way I'd genuinely never witnessed before.
Narrator: [honestly] I'd grown up assuming the sky held maybe a few hundred visible stars, based on whatever faint scattering the city allowed through its haze of light.
Narrator: [with feeling] Out there, it held thousands, layered so densely in places that the darkness between them seemed almost incidental, a mere backdrop for something far larger.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I lay back against the still-warm sand and tried, absurdly, to count them, as though counting could somehow make the scale feel more manageable.
Narrator: [reflective] I gave up almost immediately, obviously, yet the attempt itself left me strangely humbled, aware of how small my usual concerns suddenly felt.
Narrator: [gently] My uncle, who'd guided desert treks for over twenty years, told me the Bedouin used to navigate entire journeys by these same stars, trusting patterns rather than instruments.
Narrator: [curious] I asked him whether he ever grew used to this view, whether repetition eventually dulled it the way most things dull with familiarity.
Narrator: [warmly] He said the opposite happens, if anything. The more he understood about the stars' distances and ages, the more staggering the whole display became to him.
Narrator: [with feeling] Something about that struck me deeply, that knowledge here didn't diminish wonder, it deepened it, layer upon layer, the more he learned.
Narrator: [peacefully] I thought about how rarely I actually look up in ordinary life, how easily a ceiling of light pollution convinces us that this, the sliver we see, is the whole sky.
Narrator: [with a small smile] Driving home before dawn, I kept glancing at the rearview mirror, as though something that vast could somehow be left behind so easily.

quiz.question: Why did the narrator and her companions drive three hours out of the city?
options: To visit relatives
To escape the city's glow and see the stars clearly
To go camping for a work retreat
To reach a beach
quiz.explanation: They drove three hours out of the city specifically to escape its glow and see the sky.

quiz.question: What did the narrator assume about the sky before this trip?
options: That it held thousands of stars
That it held maybe a few hundred visible stars, based on the city's faint scattering
That stars were not visible at all from Earth
That she had already seen every star possible
quiz.explanation: She had grown up assuming the sky held maybe a few hundred visible stars, based on what the city's light haze allowed through.

quiz.question: How did the Bedouin, according to the uncle, use the stars?
options: To predict the weather
To navigate entire journeys, trusting patterns rather than instruments
To tell time only
They never used the stars
quiz.explanation: The uncle explained that the Bedouin used to navigate entire journeys by the stars, trusting patterns rather than instruments.

quiz.question: What did the uncle say about growing used to the view over twenty years?
options: It became boring to him
The more he understood about the stars, the more staggering the display became
He stopped looking at the sky entirely
He never noticed any change
quiz.explanation: He said the opposite of familiarity dulling wonder happens: the more he learned, the more staggering the display became.

quiz.question: What realization does the narrator have about ordinary life and the sky?
options: That the sky is not worth observing
That light pollution convinces people the small sliver they see is the whole sky
That stars only exist in deserts
That she should move to the desert permanently
quiz.explanation: She reflects on how a ceiling of light pollution convinces people that the sliver of sky they normally see is the whole sky.
